- City of Berkeley, Council item of October 11, 2022, Land Acknowledgement Recognizing Berkeley as the Ancestral, Unceded Home of the Ohlone People — https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2022-10-11%20Item%2019%20Land%20Acknowledgement%20Recognizing%20Berkeley.pdf → that in 1992 Berkeley became the first city in the United States to rename as Indigenous Peoples' Day the federal holiday formerly recognized as Columbus Day; that the change prompted revisions to the school district's history curriculum; the count of nearly 130 cities and 20 states as of 2022; Berkeley as the ancestral and unceded home of the Ohlone people, and the Confederated Villages of Lisjan and Sogorea Te' Land Trust.
- KQED, How Berkeley Became the First City to Ditch Columbus Day for Indigenous Peoples Day — https://www.kqed.org/news/11621763/how-berkeley-became-the-first-city-to-ditch-columbus-day-for-indigenous-peoples-day → the Reagan-era Christopher Columbus Quincentenary Jubilee Commission and the planned replica-ship voyage into San Francisco Bay; the formation of Resistance 500; John Curl as an organizer and his account of persuading the City Council in 1992; then-mayor Loni Hancock's recollection; Berkeley first observing the day on October 12, 1992; the annual Indigenous Peoples Day Pow Wow; that the replica-ship voyage never happened.
- Federal Register, Proclamation 10283, Indigenous Peoples' Day, 2021, 86 FR 57307 — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/10/14/2021-22583/indigenous-peoples-day-2021 → the proclamation number and its October 8, 2021 signing by President Biden; the designation of October 11, 2021; the absence of any recurring formula; the quoted references to inherent sovereignty and to trust and treaty obligations; that it does not mention Columbus Day.
- Federal Register, Proclamation 10281, Columbus Day, 2021, 86 FR 57007 — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2021-10-14/pdf/2021-22514.pdf → the separate Columbus Day proclamation signed the same day, October 8, 2021, designating the same date, October 11, 2021; the quoted acknowledgement of wrongs and atrocities inflicted on Tribal Nations and Indigenous communities.
- South Dakota Legislature, Codified Law 1-5-1.2, Native Americans' Day established — https://sdlegislature.gov/api/Statutes/1-5-1.2.html → the statutory text establishing Native Americans' Day on the second Monday in October as a legal state holiday, and its dedication to the remembrance of Native American leaders; the source note SL 1990, ch 7, section 2, giving the 1990 enactment.
- South Dakota Legislature, Codified Law 1-5-1, Holidays enumerated — https://sdlegislature.gov/api/Statutes/1-5-1.html?all=true → that the enumerated holidays include the second Monday in October as Native Americans' Day and do not include Columbus Day.
- U.S. Government Publishing Office, 5 U.S.C. 6103, 2024 edition — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title5/pdf/USCODE-2024-title5-partIII-subpartE-chap61-subchapI-sec6103.pdf → the full list of legal public holidays, which contains Columbus Day on the second Monday in October and does not contain Indigenous Peoples' Day.

name: Juneteenth
description: Juneteenth marks June 19, 1865 — the day Major General Gordon Granger issued General Order No. 3 at Galveston, informing the people of Texas that all enslaved people were free. The Emancipation Proclamation had taken effect two and a half years earlier, and the distance between those two dates is the substance of the holiday: a freedom declared and a freedom enforced are not the same thing. Texas made the day a legal state holiday in 1980; Congress added it to the federal holiday list in 2021.
body:
### History

President Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people free as of January 1, 1863, but it did not end slavery in the nation. Enforcement followed the Union Army, and the Army had not reached Texas. The Library of Congress records that Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865 "had not impacted Texas," and that many plantation owners refused to acknowledge the war was over or to release the people they held — a refusal that continued even after General Order No. 3 was issued.

Two Union arrivals changed that. On June 5, 1865, a brigade of the 25th Army Corps, more than 1,000 soldiers of African descent, captured Galveston and spread word of freedom; Civil War historians estimate that thousands of enslaved people reached freedom because of them. On June 19, Granger, commanding the Headquarters District of Texas, issued General Order No. 3 and read it to the people of Galveston.

The order is short and worth reading whole. It announces that "in accordance with a proclamation from the Executive of the United States, all slaves are free," involving "an absolute equality of personal rights and rights of property between former masters and slaves." It then advises the freed people "to remain quietly at their present homes and work for wages" and warns that they "will not be supported in idleness." The National Archives, which holds the original handwritten record, notes that the racist language of those closing sentences foreshadowed how long the fight for equal rights would run. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified later that year, made slavery unconstitutional nationwide.

### How to observe

Read General Order No. 3 in full. It takes a minute, and the National Archives prints the complete text. The closing lines, telling newly freed people not to collect at military posts and not to expect support "in idleness," are the part commemorations leave out, and they change the document's character.

Visit an emancipation ground. In many parts of Texas, freedmen and women bought land specifically for Juneteenth gatherings: Emancipation Park in Houston, purchased in 1872, is the best documented, and what is now Booker T. Washington Park in Mexia and Emancipation Park in Austin were acquired the same way.

Put red soda water on the table. The Texas State Library and Archives records it alongside prayer services, readings of the Emancipation Proclamation, accounts from formerly enslaved people, rodeos and dances in the early celebrations, which African American Texans treated like the Fourth of July. For the documentary version, the Library of Congress's Chronicling America archive holds the Dallas Herald of July 1, 1865, which printed the order two weeks after Galveston heard it.
timeline:
- January 1, 1863 — The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect, declaring enslaved people in the rebelling states free. It does not end slavery nationwide.
- June 19, 1865 — Major General Gordon Granger issues General Order No. 3 at Galveston, announcing that all enslaved people in Texas are free.
- 1866 — Large June 19 celebrations begin in Texas and continue regularly into the early twentieth century.
- 1872 — Freedmen and women in Houston purchase the land that becomes Emancipation Park, one of several Texas "emancipation grounds."
- January 1, 1980 — Texas House Bill 1016, passed by the 66th Legislature, takes effect, making June 19 a legal state holiday as Emancipation Day in Texas.
- June 17, 2021 — President Biden signs the Juneteenth National Independence Day Act, Public Law 117-17, adding Juneteenth to the federal holiday list.
faq:
Is Juneteenth a federal holiday?
Yes. The Juneteenth National Independence Day Act, Public Law 117-17, was approved June 17, 2021, inserting "Juneteenth National Independence Day, June 19" into the legal public holidays at 5 U.S.C. 6103(a), directly after Memorial Day. It is the eleventh holiday on that list and the first added since the Martin Luther King, Jr. holiday in 1983.

Why is Juneteenth on June 19 and not January 1?
January 1, 1863 is when the Emancipation Proclamation took effect; June 19, 1865 is when enforcement reached Texas. Juneteenth commemorates the second date, which is rather the point: the proclamation freed people on paper in places the Union Army did not yet control.

Did General Order No. 3 end slavery in the United States?
No. It applied to Texas. People remained enslaved in the border states that had stayed loyal to the Union, and the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified later in 1865, made slavery unconstitutional throughout the country.

When did Juneteenth become a Texas state holiday?
House Bill 1016, passed in the regular session of the 66th Texas Legislature, made June 19 a legal state holiday as "Emancipation Day in Texas," effective at the start of 1980.

name: Labor Day
description: Labor Day falls on the first Monday in September and honors the American labor movement and the people whose work built the country. It began as a union parade in New York City on a Tuesday in September 1882, spread one state legislature at a time through the 1880s, and became a federal holiday in June 1894 — in the middle of a national railroad strike that federal troops had been sent to break. The timing is part of the story, not a coincidence.
body:
### History

Who first proposed Labor Day is genuinely unsettled, and the U.S. Department of Labor says so on its own history page. One candidate is Peter J. McGuire, general secretary of the Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners and a co-founder of the American Federation of Labor, reported to have called in 1882 for a general holiday for the laboring classes. The other is Matthew Maguire, a machinist who later served as secretary of Local 344 in Paterson, New Jersey, and whom many credit with proposing the holiday that same year while secretary of the Central Labor Union in New York. A Paterson newspaper called Maguire "the undisputed author of Labor Day as a holiday." The near-identical surnames have not helped, and the Labor Department declines to pick.

What is documented is the event. The Central Labor Union held the first Labor Day in New York City on Tuesday, September 5, 1882, and a second a year later on the same date. The plan was a street parade showing the strength and esprit de corps of a community's trade and labor organizations, followed by a festival for workers and their families. Speeches came later.

The states moved first. Oregon passed the first Labor Day law on February 21, 1887; Colorado, Massachusetts, New Jersey and New York followed within the year, and Connecticut, Nebraska and Pennsylvania by the decade's end. By 1894 another 23 states had adopted it.

Congress acted mid-strike. The Pullman strike ran from May 11 to July 20, 1894; President Grover Cleveland declared it a federal crime and sent troops, and two men were killed. On June 28, 1894, Congress made the first Monday in September a legal holiday and Cleveland signed it. The Library of Congress connects that speed to the need to calm tensions after the deaths.

### How to observe

Read the Department of Labor's own history of the holiday. It is short, and it refuses to settle who founded Labor Day — which makes it a better document than most of what is written about the day.

Visit Pullman National Historical Park if you are near Chicago. The planned industrial town at the center of the 1894 strike still stands as a neighborhood, and the Park Service runs a visitor center at 610 E. 111th Street. The holiday and the strike are the same year; standing in one explains the other.

Look up what your own town did. The Library of Congress's Chronicling America holds digitized American newspapers published through 1963 from nearly every state and territory. Searching your city against the 1880s and 1890s turns up the parades, picnics and arguments as they were reported — the only way to see a holiday that arrived one state at a time.
timeline:
- September 5, 1882 — The Central Labor Union holds the first Labor Day in New York City, on a Tuesday: a street parade followed by a festival for workers and their families.
- September 5, 1883 — The Central Labor Union holds its second Labor Day on the same date.
- February 21, 1887 — Oregon passes the first state Labor Day law. Colorado, Massachusetts, New Jersey and New York follow the same year.
- May 11, 1894 — The Pullman strike begins, running until July 20. Cleveland declares it a federal crime and sends troops; two men are killed.
- June 28, 1894 — Congress makes the first Monday in September a legal holiday and President Grover Cleveland signs it. By then 23 more states had adopted the holiday.
- June 28, 1968 — The Uniform Monday Holiday Act (Pub. L. 90-363) reworks the federal calendar, adding Columbus Day and moving Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day and Veterans Day. Labor Day is not among the holidays it changes.
faq:
Is Labor Day a federal holiday?
Yes. It is one of the eleven legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103, observed on the first Monday in September. Federal offices, banks and post offices close.

Who invented Labor Day?
Nobody knows for certain, and the Department of Labor says so. The two candidates are Peter J. McGuire, general secretary of the Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners, and Matthew Maguire, a machinist from Paterson, New Jersey. Both are tied to proposals in 1882, and the nearly identical surnames have kept the question open ever since.

When was the first Labor Day?
Tuesday, September 5, 1882, in New York City, organized by the Central Labor Union. It was a parade and a festival, not a day off.

Why is Labor Day in September rather than May 1?
There is no primary source for that decision in the record this page relies on, so it will not guess at one. What is documented is that the September date came from the Central Labor Union's 1882 celebration and was already law in more than twenty states before Congress adopted it in 1894.

When did Labor Day become a federal holiday?
June 28, 1894. Congress made the first Monday in September a legal holiday and President Cleveland signed it, during the Pullman strike that his own administration had sent troops to break.

L. 90-363 of June 28, 1968 showing which holidays it changed.

The Department of Labor page and the Library of Congress guide differ slightly in wording on June 28, 1894 — Labor says Cleveland signed the act, the Library says the holiday was "approved" — and this page follows the Department of Labor as the more specific of the two.

name: Mardi Gras
description: Mardi Gras is Shrove Tuesday, the day immediately before Ash Wednesday, and the last day of the Carnival season. In Louisiana it is not a figure of speech but a statutory one: state law lists "the day of Mardi Gras" among the state's days of public rest and legal holidays. Almost everything Americans picture when they hear the word — krewes, floats, purple and green and gold — was worked out in New Orleans between the 1850s and the 1880s.
body:
### History

The name is French for Fat Tuesday, which Britannica traces to "the custom of using all the fats in the home before Lent." Shrove Tuesday is "the day immediately preceding Ash Wednesday (the beginning of Lent in Western Christian churches)." Pinned to Ash Wednesday rather than to a calendar date, the day moves every year; the New Orleans Public Library's City Archives publish the dates from 1947 through 2050.

Louisiana dates its own connection to 1699. "Since 1699, when Pierre Le Moyne, Sieur d'Iberville celebrated his arrival at the mouth of the Mississippi on Shrove Tuesday, Mardi Gras has been integrally linked to Louisiana's cultural heritage," the Louisiana State Museum writes. Evidence for the century that follows is thin — the museum notes "scant evidence of Carnival during the early 1700s" — but by 1781 the season was established enough that Spanish colonial authorities forbade free people of color and enslaved people to mask or mimic whites during it. The first parades were improvised, "impromptu processions formed by maskers already in the streets," with young Creole men organizing informal processions by the 1830s.

The modern machinery arrives in the 1850s. The City Archives date the Mistick Krewe of Comus to 1856 and record that "the first Mardi Gras parade was held in 1857, featuring the Mistick Krewe of Comus"; the state museum instead describes the krewe as emerging in 1857, and both years are reported below rather than reconciled. Comus staged a nighttime procession followed by a private ball, and set the pattern for everything after it, secrecy included: "the aura of mystery and surprise associated with krewes to this day was conceived by Comus."

Others followed quickly: the Twelfth Night Revelers in 1870, the Knights of Momus and Rex in 1872, the Krewe of Proteus in 1882. Rex supplied the parts that now read as official, billing its monarchs as the king and queen of Carnival and introducing a daytime parade. Purple, green and gold, the City Archives state, "are the official colors of carnival and represent justice, faith, and power."

The sharpest modern break came in 1992, when the city tied parade permits to Councilmember Dorothy Mae Taylor's ordinance barring discrimination in krewe membership. Comus, Momus and Proteus all stopped parading that year; Proteus resumed in 2000, and the Comus and Momus parades never returned.

### How to observe

Find out whether you actually have the day off, because the answer is unusually technical. Louisiana lists "the day of Mardi Gras" among its statewide legal holidays and names it for state employees, but local closure is a separate question: the statute names twenty-nine parishes, plus all municipalities, where "Mardi Gras shall be a holiday when the governing authorities so declare by ordinance."

Leave the French Quarter. Rex, the King of Carnival, parades Mardi Gras morning, and the mayor of New Orleans traditionally toasts the kings and queens of Rex and Zulu on the steps of Gallier Hall.

For the older tradition rather than the spectacle, go to a rural courir, or run — "a seemingly chaotic quest to obtain ingredients for a communal gumbo" that in fact "involves a complex system of rules." Because courirs were held in isolated areas where illiteracy was prevalent, the state museum notes, "the historical record is sketchy."
timeline:
- 1699 — Pierre Le Moyne, Sieur d'Iberville celebrates his arrival at the mouth of the Mississippi on Shrove Tuesday.
- 1781 — Spanish colonial authorities forbid free people of color and enslaved people to mask or mimic whites during the Carnival season.
- 1857 — The first Mardi Gras parade, staged by the Mistick Krewe of Comus, which the City Archives date to 1856.
- 1872 — Rex and the Knights of Momus are founded; Rex introduces a daytime parade and the king and queen of Carnival.
- 1896 — Les Mysterieuses becomes the first large-scale women's krewe.
- 1992 — A city ordinance ties parade permits to non-discrimination in krewe membership; Comus, Momus and Proteus stop parading. Proteus returns in 2000.
faq:
When is Mardi Gras?
It has no fixed date. Mardi Gras is Shrove Tuesday, the day immediately before Ash Wednesday, so it moves each year with the start of Lent. The New Orleans Public Library's City Archives publish the dates from 1947 through 2050.

Is Mardi Gras a public holiday?
In Louisiana, yes: the statute listing the state's days of public rest and legal holidays includes "the day of Mardi Gras," and state departments are told that no employee shall work on it insofar as practicable. Local closures depend on local action, since the same statute lets twenty-nine named parishes and all municipalities declare it a holiday by ordinance. It is not among the 11 federal holidays in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a).

What do purple, green and gold mean?
They are the official colors of Carnival, and the City Archives give their meanings as justice, faith and power.

What is a krewe?
A private Carnival organization that stages a parade, a ball, or both. The oldest — Comus, the Twelfth Night Revelers, Momus, Rex and Proteus — are known as the old line krewes, and three of them stopped parading in 1992.

name: Martin Luther King, Jr. Day
description: The federal holiday on the third Monday in January is, in the statute, the Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr. — though almost everyone says Martin Luther King, Jr. Day. It took fifteen years to create: a bill was introduced four days after King was killed in 1968 and died without a vote, and the law establishing the holiday was not signed until November 2, 1983. Since 1994 federal law has also pointed the day toward community service, which makes it one of the few American holidays with an instruction attached.
body:
### History

Representative John Conyers of Michigan introduced the first bill to make King's birthday a national holiday four days after the assassination, in April 1968. Congress took no action. The campaign that eventually won ran another fifteen years and was fought in public more than in committee: Stevie Wonder's 1980 song "Happy Birthday" became its anthem, Coretta Scott King testified repeatedly, millions signed petitions, and marches in Washington in 1982 and 1983 kept the pressure on.

The bill passed both houses in 1983. President Ronald Reagan signed Public Law 98-144 on November 2, 1983, amending section 6103(a) of title 5 of the United States Code to insert a new line immediately below New Year's Day: the Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr., the third Monday in January. The law deliberately delayed itself — the amendment took effect on January 1, 1986, more than two years after enactment. In August 1984 Reagan established a commission to prepare the first observance, and he proclaimed Monday, January 20, 1986 as the first Martin Luther King, Jr. Day.

The states moved at their own pace. South Carolina did not make the third Monday in January a regular state holiday — rather than an optional one state employees could take in place of a Confederate holiday — until an act ratified on April 26, 2000.

The service dimension came later still. On August 23, 1994, President Bill Clinton signed the King Holiday and Service Act, authorizing the Corporation for National and Community Service, in consultation with the Martin Luther King, Jr. Federal Holiday Commission, to fund service projects on the holiday reflecting King's legacy — among them "cooperation and understanding among racial and ethnic groups, nonviolent conflict resolution, equal economic and educational opportunities, and social justice."

### How to observe

Read King himself rather than quotations of him. The long pieces — the letter from the Birmingham jail, the later speeches on poverty and war — are the ones holiday programming skips in favor of four lines from 1963.

Serve, if there is something near you worth doing. The 1994 act built grant-funded projects into the day, but almost all of it is organized locally — a city volunteer office, a school district, a congregation, a food bank. Listings go up in the first week of January and the useful ones fill fast.

Visit Martin Luther King, Jr. National Historical Park in Atlanta. It holds King's birth home, the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church where he and his father preached, and the tomb of Dr. and Mrs. King on a brick island in a reflecting pool. Ranger-led programs are free. Birth home tours take fifteen people at a time, hourly from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and you register in person at Historic Fire Station No. 6 — so arrive early.
timeline:
- April 1968 — Four days after King's assassination, Rep. John Conyers of Michigan introduces the first bill to make his birthday a national holiday. Congress takes no action.
- 1980 — Stevie Wonder releases "Happy Birthday," which becomes the campaign's rallying song; marches in Washington in 1982 and 1983 build on it.
- November 2, 1983 — President Ronald Reagan signs Public Law 98-144, adding the Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr. to 5 U.S.C. 6103 as the third Monday in January, effective January 1, 1986.
- August 27, 1984 — Reagan establishes a commission to prepare the first observance of the new holiday.
- January 20, 1986 — The first Martin Luther King, Jr. Day is observed, two days after Reagan's proclamation naming the date.
- August 23, 1994 — President Bill Clinton signs the King Holiday and Service Act, authorizing federal grants for service projects on the holiday.
faq:
What is the official name of the holiday?
The Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr. That is how 5 U.S.C. 6103 lists it. "Martin Luther King, Jr. Day" is the common name and the one Reagan used in the 1986 proclamation.

Is the holiday on King's actual birthday?
No. King was born on January 15, 1929. The holiday is the third Monday in January, which can only fall between January 15 and January 21, so it lands on his birthday only in years when January 15 happens to be a Monday.

Why did it take fifteen years?
Conyers' 1968 bill died without action and no measure cleared both houses until 1983. The White House's own account credits public pressure rather than legislative maneuvering: Stevie Wonder's "Happy Birthday," Coretta Scott King's repeated testimony, millions of petition signatures, and the 1982 and 1983 marches in Washington.

Is it a day off or a day of service?
Both, legally. It is a federal legal public holiday, so federal offices close. The King Holiday and Service Act of 1994 separately authorized federal grants for service projects on the day, which is why much of what happens is volunteer work rather than ceremony.

Do all states observe it?
It is a federal holiday, so federal offices close everywhere. State practice took much longer to converge: South Carolina made the third Monday in January a regular rather than optional state holiday only in 2000, by an act ratified that April.

The claim that South Carolina was the last state to adopt the holiday is widely repeated but is not asserted here, because the South Carolina act does not say so and no primary source for the ranking was found.

name: Memorial Day
description: Memorial Day falls on the last Monday in May and honors Americans who died in military service — which is the distinction that matters, because Veterans Day honors everyone who served. It began as Decoration Day, a Civil War observance of strewing flowers on graves, and carried both names for most of a century. Where it started first is genuinely disputed, and the federal government's own answer is not the only credible one.
body:
### History

The holiday's official origin is a general order. On May 5, 1868, John A. Logan, commander-in-chief of the Grand Army of the Republic — the Union veterans' organization — issued General Orders No. 11, setting aside May 30 for "strewing with flowers or otherwise decorating the graves of comrades" and asking that the country guard those graves "with sacred vigilance." Late May was chosen for the flowers: the order wanted "the choicest flowers of springtime." Logan's adjutant general, Norton P. Chipman, drafted it; Logan added several paragraphs of his own.

The first national observance followed on May 30, 1868, at Arlington National Cemetery, on grounds that then held roughly 11,250 Union dead, Black and white, and about 350 Confederate dead, more than half of them unknown. General and Mrs. Ulysses S. Grant were among those presiding, James A. Garfield — then both a general and a congressman — spoke, and the Department of Veterans Affairs puts the crowd at about 5,000.

The practice was older than the order, and the claims are crowded. Southern women were decorating soldiers' graves before the war ended, with precedents recorded in Mississippi, Virginia and South Carolina by 1865. On April 25, 1866, a women's memorial association in Columbus, Mississippi, decorated Confederate graves and the neglected Union graves beside them. Waterloo, New York, holds the federal title — Congress and President Lyndon Johnson named it the birthplace of Memorial Day in 1966, for observances beginning May 5, 1866 — while Boalsburg, Carbondale, Macon, Columbus and Richmond all have claims of their own. Earlier still, on May 1, 1865, freed Black residents of Charleston, South Carolina, together with soldiers of the 35th and 104th United States Colored Troops and the 54th Massachusetts Infantry, gathered at the city's old racetrack to honor and decorate the graves of 257 Union prisoners of war whom the retreating Confederate army had buried there in haste. The National Park Service calls it one of the earliest recorded observances and says the question of which came first is still debated.

Decoration Day gave way to Memorial Day around the turn of the twentieth century, without a decisive moment. The Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 took effect in 1971, moving the holiday to the last Monday in May and extending it to Americans who died in all the nation's wars; a few states still mark May 30. In December 2000 the National Moment of Remembrance Act created the commission behind a minute of silence at 3 p.m. local time.

### How to observe

Take the 3 p.m. minute. It is the one part of this holiday with a fixed national time, and, unlike a parade, it asks nothing but that you stop.

Visit a national cemetery instead of a sale. The Department of Veterans Affairs' National Cemetery Administration keeps cemeteries in most states and publishes their locations; many hold a ceremony and a flag placement over the holiday weekend.

Read Logan's order. It is short, it is the document the holiday rests on, and its instruction — that the graves be guarded "with sacred vigilance" and kept tended for the generations that follow — is a plainer statement of the point than most of what gets said on the day.
timeline:
- May 1, 1865 — Freed Black residents of Charleston, South Carolina, with Black and white Union troops, honor and decorate the graves of 257 Union prisoners of war at the city's old racetrack — among the earliest recorded observances.
- May 5, 1866 — Waterloo, New York, begins the annual observance that Congress and President Johnson would cite in 1966 in naming it the birthplace of Memorial Day.
- May 5, 1868 — John A. Logan, commander-in-chief of the Grand Army of the Republic, issues General Orders No. 11, setting May 30 aside for decorating the graves of the war dead.
- May 30, 1868 — The first national Decoration Day is held at Arlington National Cemetery, with the Grants among those presiding and James A. Garfield speaking.
- 1971 — The Uniform Monday Holiday Act takes effect, moving the holiday to the last Monday in May and extending it to the dead of all American wars.
- December 2000 — The National Moment of Remembrance Act (Public Law 106-579) establishes the commission behind the 3 p.m. minute of silence.
faq:
Is Memorial Day a federal holiday?
Yes. It is one of the eleven legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103 and falls on the last Monday in May, so its date moves between May 25 and May 31.

What is the difference between Memorial Day and Veterans Day?
Memorial Day honors military personnel who died in service, particularly those killed in battle or from wounds sustained in battle. Veterans Day, on November 11, honors everyone who served honorably, and is largely a day for thanking living veterans.

Where did Memorial Day start?
There is no settled answer. The federal government named Waterloo, New York the birthplace in 1966; the National Park Service records a May 1, 1865 observance in Charleston, South Carolina as one of the earliest; and Boalsburg, Carbondale, Columbus, Macon and Richmond all have claims. What is documented is the start of the national observance: Logan's order of May 5, 1868 and the ceremony at Arlington that May 30.

When did Memorial Day stop being May 30?
The Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 took effect in 1971, moving the observance to the last Monday in May and extending it to Americans who died in all the nation's wars. A few states still mark May 30.

What is the National Moment of Remembrance?
A minute of silence at 3 p.m. local time on Memorial Day. The National Moment of Remembrance Act of December 2000 created the White House commission that endorsed it.

name: Mother's Day
description: Mother's Day falls on the second Sunday in May, a date Congress fixed in 1914, and it was the work of one woman who spent much of the rest of her life objecting to what it became. Anna Jarvis built it as a memorial to her own mother and insisted on the singular possessive: one mother, your mother, not a general tribute to motherhood. The apostrophe held. Almost nothing else she wanted did.
body:
### History

Unusually for an American holiday, this one has a documented founder and a documented first day. Anna Maria Jarvis was born in Webster, West Virginia, on May 1, 1864. Her mother, Ann Reeves Jarvis, had organized Mothers' Day Work Clubs that cared for sick and wounded soldiers from both sides during the Civil War, and afterward arranged a Mother's Friendship Day meant to bring together the mothers of Union and Confederate veterans. When Ann died in 1905, her daughter began campaigning for a national day in her memory.

The first formal Mother's Day service was held on May 10, 1908, at Andrews Methodist Episcopal Church in Grafton, West Virginia. Jarvis herself was not there — she was at a Mother's Day event at Wanamaker's in Philadelphia — but she sent 500 white carnations for the congregation. Philadelphia newspaper publishers promoted the second Sunday in May, West Virginia passed a law recognizing the day in 1910, and other states followed.

Congress acted on May 8, 1914, with a joint resolution, H.J. Res. 263, entered in the statutes as Public Resolution No. 25 and titled "Designating the second Sunday in May as Mother's Day, and for other purposes." Woodrow Wilson issued the proclamation the next day, asking Americans to display the flag in honor of mothers whose sons had died in war.

What followed is the part Jarvis is least remembered for. She spent her later years opposing the holiday's commercial turn, objecting to florists who raised carnation prices for the occasion and to standardized greeting cards, which she regarded as a way of not writing to your mother. She died on November 24, 1948, in West Chester, Pennsylvania, at 84, having outlived her own holiday's original form by decades.

### How to observe

Write something. Jarvis's specific complaint about printed cards was that buying one is a way of avoiding the harder thing, and she is the person who built the holiday, so the objection carries some weight.

Find out about the woman the day is actually for. The original Mother's Day was a memorial service for one person, held by a daughter who had lost her, and the questions you can only ask while someone is alive are the ones the holiday was invented around.

The Grafton church where that first service was held still stands as the International Mother's Day Shrine; the National Park Service documents its place in the holiday's history and the Library of Congress holds photographs of it.

And if you want the holiday's arrival as it was actually reported, the Library of Congress's Chronicling America guide to Mother's Day collects newspaper coverage from 1908 onward. The years between 1908 and 1914 show a holiday being argued into existence rather than handed down.
timeline:
- 1905 — Ann Reeves Jarvis dies; her daughter Anna begins campaigning for a national day in her memory.
- May 10, 1908 — The first formal Mother's Day service is held at Andrews Methodist Episcopal Church in Grafton, West Virginia; Jarvis sends 500 white carnations.
- 1910 — West Virginia passes a law designating the holiday, and other states follow.
- May 8, 1914 — Congress passes H.J. Res. 263, Public Resolution No. 25, designating the second Sunday in May as Mother's Day.
- May 9, 1914 — Woodrow Wilson proclaims the first national Mother's Day, asking Americans to display the flag.
- November 24, 1948 — Anna Jarvis dies in West Chester, Pennsylvania, after years of opposing the holiday's commercialization.
faq:
Why is it "Mother's Day" and not "Mothers' Day"?
Because the singular possessive was the point. Jarvis meant a day for each person's own mother rather than a tribute to mothers in general, and the 1914 joint resolution uses that spelling in its title.

Is Mother's Day a federal holiday?
No. Federal holidays are set by law, under 5 U.S.C. 6103, and Mother's Day is not among them. The 1914 resolution designated the day and asked for the flag to be displayed; it did not create a day off.

Who founded Mother's Day?
Anna Maria Jarvis, born in Webster, West Virginia, on May 1, 1864. She began campaigning after her mother's death in 1905, the first service was held in 1908, and Congress designated the day in 1914.

Did the founder really turn against the holiday?
Yes. The National Park Service records her objecting to florists raising carnation prices for the occasion and to standardized greeting cards.

Is Mother's Day the same date everywhere?
No. Many countries observe it on the American date, the second Sunday in May, while others mark a day for mothers at a different time of year entirely, with separate origins.

name: New Year's Day
description: New Year's Day falls on January 1, which is an administrative decision rather than a fact of nature. The date has been moved, abandoned, and restored more than once in Western Europe — Britain and its American colonies did not adopt it until 1752 — and most of what Americans actually do on the day, from the parade in Pasadena to the ball in Times Square, was invented between 1788 and 1907.
body:
### History

January 1 has no astronomical claim on the new year. Tradition credits Numa Pompilius, around 715 to 673 BCE, with reordering the Roman calendar so that January replaced March as the first month, though that attribution is traditional rather than documented; there is evidence that January 1 was not made the official start of the Roman year until 153 BCE. Julius Caesar's reform of 46 BCE produced the Julian calendar, which kept January 1 as the year's opening date.

Then it moved. After the fifth century much of Christian Europe shifted the new year off January 1, and March 25 and December 25 both became common starting dates. Pope Gregory XIII's calendar of 1582 restored January 1; Italy, France, and Spain adopted it immediately, while Protestant and Orthodox countries took far longer. Britain and its American colonies did not switch until 1752, having kept New Year's Day on March 25 until then — which makes the January 1 holiday younger, in English-speaking America, than most of the colonies observing it.

Legal standing is younger still. Congress first established public holidays in 1870, for the District of Columbia: New Year's Day, Independence Day, Christmas, and Thanksgiving.

The two American set pieces are both promotional in origin and both well documented. Times Square got its crowd in 1904, when Adolph Ochs staged an all-day street festival with fireworks to mark the opening of The New York Times' new headquarters — he had already persuaded the city to rename Longacre Square after the paper — and more than 200,000 people came. The city banned the fireworks two years later, and in 1907 a lighted ball descended the flagpole atop One Times Square instead: iron and wood, five feet across, 700 pounds, one hundred 25-watt bulbs, built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr. It has gone down every year since except 1942 and 1943, when New York's wartime dimout darkened the square. The ball unveiled in November 2025 is 12.5 feet across and weighs 12,350 pounds.

Pasadena's parade is older and was frank about its purpose. Members of the Valley Hunt Club, led by Charles Frederick Holder, staged the first Tournament of Roses on New Year's Day in 1890. Holder's pitch to the club was advertising copy: "In New York, people are buried in snow. Let's hold a festival to tell the world about our paradise."

### How to observe

Find out when your New Year's Day off actually falls. Federal employees follow 5 U.S.C. 6103, and when January 1 lands on a Saturday the holiday is observed the preceding Friday. The federal New Year's Day for 2028 is therefore Friday, December 31, 2027.

Sing the song wrong knowingly. Robert Burns did not so much write "Auld Lang Syne" as compile it, in 1788, from older material reaching back as far as the sixteenth century. The tune was his publisher's choice and derives from a traditional Scottish folk-dance tune, possibly Sir Alexander Don's strathspey, though the Library of Congress notes the exact source is difficult to establish.

Watch the Rose Parade knowing what it was for. The Tournament of Roses began in 1890 as a winter-climate advertisement for Southern California, and the man who proposed it said so out loud at the meeting that launched it.
timeline:
- 153 BCE — Evidence indicates January 1 becomes the official start of the Roman year.
- 46 BCE — Julius Caesar's reform produces the Julian calendar, which keeps January 1 as the year's opening date.
- 1582 — Pope Gregory XIII's calendar restores January 1; Italy, France, and Spain adopt it immediately.
- 1752 — Britain and its American colonies adopt the Gregorian calendar, having observed New Year's Day on March 25 until then.
- 1870 — Congress establishes the first federal public holidays for the District of Columbia, New Year's Day among them.
- 1907 — A lighted ball descends One Times Square for the first time, after the city banned the fireworks of the 1904 celebration.
faq:
Is New Year's Day a federal holiday?
Yes, and one of the original four. Congress first established public holidays in 1870 — New Year's Day, Independence Day, Christmas, and Thanksgiving — for the District of Columbia. It is now listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103.

What happens when January 1 falls on a weekend?
Federal employees observe the holiday on the nearest weekday: the preceding Friday when January 1 is a Saturday, the following Monday when it is a Sunday. January 1, 2028 is a Saturday, so the federal observance is Friday, December 31, 2027.

Why does the year start on January 1?
Because it was legislated that way, repeatedly. Rome appears to have fixed January 1 as the official new year by 153 BCE, and the Julian calendar of 46 BCE kept it. Medieval Christian Europe largely moved the date to March 25 or December 25. The Gregorian calendar of 1582 restored January 1, and Britain and its colonies followed only in 1752.

Has the Times Square ball ever not dropped?
Twice. It was not lowered in 1942 or 1943, when New York's wartime dimout darkened the square. Crowds gathered anyway and marked midnight with a minute of silence and chimes rung from sound trucks at the base of the tower.

Where do New Year's resolutions come from?
The custom is usually traced to Babylonian or Roman vow-making, but that lineage is asserted far more often than it is documented, and this page has no primary source for it. Resolving at the turn of the year is an old habit; its specific ancestry is not established.

name: New Year's Eve
description: New Year's Eve is December 31, and in the United States it holds two very different midnights. One is a commercial spectacle a newspaper owner invented in 1904 to publicize his new building. The other is a vigil that Black congregations have kept since the night of December 31, 1862, when people waited in the dark for the Emancipation Proclamation to take effect.
body:
### History

The Times Square version began as advertising, and the Times Square Alliance, which runs the celebration today, says so plainly. Adolph Ochs, the German Jewish immigrant who owned The New York Times, had persuaded the city to rename Longacre Square after his paper in 1904. That December he marked the opening of the Times Tower with an all-day street festival ending in fireworks shot from the base of the building, and more than 200,000 people came.

The city banned the fireworks two years later. Ochs's replacement was a lighted ball lowered down the tower's flagpole at midnight to begin 1908, built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr: iron and wood, five feet across, 700 pounds, lit by one hundred 25-watt bulbs. Starr's company, Artkraft Strauss, lowered it for most of the century that followed. The ball changed with its materials — wrought iron in 1920, aluminum in 1955, crystal in 2000, LEDs in 2007 — and the one unveiled in November 2025 is 12.5 feet across and weighs 12,350 pounds. It has descended every year since 1907 except 1942 and 1943, when New York's wartime dimout darkened the square; crowds gathered anyway and marked midnight with a minute of silence and chimes rung from sound trucks at the tower's base.

The other American tradition is quieter and was built on far higher stakes. Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on September 22, 1862, declaring enslaved people in the rebelling states free — but it would not take effect until the new year. So on the night of December 31, 1862, as the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture records, enslaved and free African Americans gathered, many of them in secret, to wait. The proclamation took effect at midnight, at the start of January 1, 1863, and the night became known as Watch Night, or Freedom's Eve.

Gathering at all carried risk: Georgia's slave code of 1848 barred people of color from preaching or joining a religious meeting where more than seven were present. People worshipped anyway, in plantation praise houses and in "hush harbors" out in the woods, and the museum records the account of Charlotte Martin, a formerly enslaved woman in Florida whose brother was beaten to death for taking part. Watch Night services are still kept, generally beginning around 7 p.m. and running through midnight.

### How to observe

Look for a Watch Night service. They are widely held and generally open, and the history above is why the room goes quiet in the minutes before midnight rather than loud.

Do not plan the night around a federal day off: December 31 is not a federal holiday, and reaches that calendar only when January 1 falls on a Saturday. The next of those is 2028.

Arrange the ride before you drink. NHTSA counted 11,904 deaths in drunk-driving crashes in 2024, about 32 a day. It publishes no New Year's Eve-specific figure, so treat the familiar "deadliest night of the year" line with suspicion.
timeline:
- September 22, 1862 — Lincoln issues the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in the rebelling states free, to take effect with the new year.
- December 31, 1862 — African Americans gather, many in secret, to await its effect; the night becomes known as Watch Night, or Freedom's Eve. The proclamation takes effect at midnight on January 1, 1863.
- 1904 — Adolph Ochs marks the opening of the Times Tower with an all-day festival ending in fireworks; more than 200,000 people attend.
- 1907 — With the fireworks banned, a lighted ball descends the Times Tower flagpole to begin 1908: iron and wood, five feet across, 700 pounds, built by Jacob Starr.
- 1942–1943 — The ball is not lowered, because of New York's wartime dimout; crowds mark midnight with a minute of silence and chimes.
- November 2025 — The newest ball is unveiled: 12.5 feet across, 12,350 pounds.
faq:
Is New Year's Eve a federal holiday?
No. The Office of Personnel Management lists eleven legal public holidays under 5 U.S.C. 6103 and December 31 is not among them. It reaches the federal calendar only as the in-lieu-of date for New Year's Day when January 1 falls on a Saturday, as it does in 2028.

What is Watch Night?
A New Year's Eve service rooted in the night of December 31, 1862, when enslaved and free African Americans gathered, often in secret, to wait for the Emancipation Proclamation to take effect at midnight on January 1, 1863. Services are still held, generally beginning around 7 p.m. and running through midnight.

Has the Times Square ball ever failed to drop?
Twice, in 1942 and 1943, when New York's wartime dimout darkened the square. Crowds gathered anyway and marked midnight with a minute of silence and chimes rung from sound trucks at the base of the tower.

Why did the ball drop start in the first place?
Because the city banned the fireworks. Adolph Ochs's 1904 celebration for the opening of the Times Tower ended in a fireworks display, which was prohibited two years later, so to begin 1908 he had a lighted ball lowered down the tower's flagpole instead.

Cited as the organizer of the event and so the primary source for its own history.
- Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture, The Historical Legacy of Watch Night — https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/stories/historical-legacy-watch-night → Lincoln's September 22, 1862 order declaring enslaved people in the rebelling Confederate states free and its delayed effect; the gathering on the night of December 31, 1862, many in secret, and the names Watch Night and "Freedom's Eve"; the proclamation taking effect at midnight at the start of January 1, 1863; praying, worshipping, singing and dancing at the first Watch Night; the 1848 Georgia slave code barring people of color from preaching or joining religious gatherings of more than seven; plantation praise houses and "hush harbors"; Charlotte Martin's account of her brother beaten to death for taking part; modern services beginning around 7 p.m. and running through midnight; the New Year's Day meal of collard greens for prosperity and Hoppin' John, and the black-eyed pea reaching the Carolinas in the early 1700s.
- U.S. Office of Personnel Management, Federal Holidays — https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/federal-holidays/ → the eleven legal public holidays established by 5 U.S.C. 6103 and the absence of December 31 from that list; December 31 appearing on the federal calendar only as the observed date for New Year's Day when January 1 falls on a Saturday, including 2028; the Saturday-to-preceding-Friday rule under 5 U.S.C. 6103(b).

NHTSA publishes no New Year's Eve-specific breakdown on this page, which is why no such figure is given above.

Note on a source inconsistency: the Times Square Alliance page states that seven Ball versions have been designed while also calling the Constellation Ball the ninth Ball, and does not reconcile the two. This page therefore gives no count of how many balls there have been, and cites only the individual balls and dates the page states directly.

Rejected as sources: nationaltoday, nationaldaycalendar, checkiday, timeanddate, and content-farm or AI-generated listicles.

description: Patriot Day falls on September 11 and honors the 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks of 2001. Congress designated it by joint resolution in December of that year, which means the first Patriot Day was September 11, 2002. It is a day of remembrance and, since 2009, of service; it is not a holiday, and nothing closes.
body:
### History

The designation came quickly. House Joint Resolution 71 passed the House on October 25, 2001 and the Senate on November 30, and was approved on December 18 as Public Law 107-89. Its operative language, now at 36 U.S.C. 144, is four words: "September 11 is Patriot Day." The rest of the statute asks the president to issue a proclamation each year calling on governments and the public to observe the day, on federal agencies to fly the flag at half-staff, and on Americans to observe a moment of silence. The statute names no time for that silence.

An earlier proclamation is sometimes mistaken for the first Patriot Day. Proclamation 7462, signed September 13, 2001, designated Friday, September 14 as a National Day of Prayer and Remembrance, with "noontime memorial services, the ringing of bells at that hour, and evening candlelight remembrance vigils." That was a single day, not an annual observance.

The service half of the day arrived eight years later, and the law behind it is usually described wrongly. The Edward M. Kennedy Serve America Act, Public Law 111-13 of April 21, 2009, does not amend the Patriot Day statute and does not contain the word "Patriot" anywhere. What it did was add a provision to the national service laws authorizing the federal service agency, now AmeriCorps, to organize activities and make grants for "the September 11th National Day of Service and Remembrance" — an observance the 2009 proclamation credited to the victims' families. So "Patriot Day and National Day of Service and Remembrance" is the title of a presidential proclamation, not the day's name in statute — and administrations have used that longer title inconsistently.

The 8:46 a.m. Eastern moment of silence also comes from the proclamations rather than the law; it marks the time American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower. The 2002 proclamation asked for silence "beginning at 8:46 a.m. eastern daylight time, or another appropriate commemorative time"; the 2009 one dropped the alternative, and recent proclamations have directed half-staff without naming a time at all.

### How to observe

The 9/11 Memorial maintains a searchable directory of every name inscribed on the bronze parapets, which locates a person by panel. Reading one entry, rather than a total, is the closest thing to the point of the day.

For the service half, AmeriCorps runs a volunteer search for projects tied to September 11, and the nonprofit 9/11 Day organizes meal-packing events that produced more than 6.5 million meals across eighteen cities in 2023. If you want primary material, the Library of Congress's September 11, 2001 Documentary Project holds oral histories recorded in the weeks after the attacks, with roughly 200 interviews online. The Flight 93 National Memorial near Shanksville and the Pentagon Memorial, with its 184 benches, are both open to visitors.
timeline:
- 2001 — Public Law 107-89, approved December 18, designates September 11 as Patriot Day; it is codified at 36 U.S.C. 144.
- 2002 — The first Patriot Day is observed on September 11 under Proclamation 7590.
- 2008 — The Pentagon Memorial, a bench for each of the 184 people killed there, is dedicated on September 11.
- 2009 — The Serve America Act authorizes federal support for a September 11 National Day of Service and Remembrance.
- 2011 — The 9/11 Memorial is dedicated on the tenth anniversary and opens to the public the next day.
faq:
Is Patriot Day a federal holiday?

No. The eleven legal public holidays are listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103, and Patriot Day is not among them. It sits in Title 36, the patriotic observances title, so no federal leave attaches.

How many people were killed?

The 9/11 Memorial counts 2,977 people killed at the three attack sites on September 11, 2001: 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon, and 40 aboard Flight 93. That figure counts victims and excludes the nineteen hijackers. The memorial bears 2,983 names, because it also honors the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. Among the 2,977 were 441 first responders from more than thirty agencies, including 343 New York City firefighters, 37 Port Authority police officers and 23 New York City police officers.

How many have died since of 9/11-related illness?

There is no official count. The federal World Trade Center Health Program states plainly that it does not track cause of death for its members, so its figures cannot answer the question. The Justice Department's Victim Compensation Fund reported 8,996 claims filed on behalf of people who had died as of December 31, 2025, but a claim is not a certified cause of death.

Is Patriot Day the same as Patriots' Day?

No. Patriots' Day is a state holiday in Massachusetts and Maine observed on the third Monday in April, commemorating the battles of Lexington and Concord in 1775.

What time is the moment of silence?

Proclamations have commonly set it at 8:46 a.m. Eastern, the moment of the first impact, though the statute itself names no time and recent proclamations have directed only that flags fly at half-staff.

name: Presidents' Day
description: The federal holiday on the third Monday in February is, in law, Washington's Birthday. Congress has never renamed it: "Presidents' Day" was proposed in 1951, got nowhere officially, and became the common name three decades later through holiday sales advertising. The holiday also cannot land on Washington's birthday — the third Monday in February falls between the 15th and the 21st, and he was born on the 22nd.
body:
### History

February 22 became a holiday for federal employees in the District of Columbia by an act of January 31, 1879. That law did not require that anyone be paid for the day off; an 1885 act fixed that, requiring pay for federal holidays and extending them to federal employees everywhere rather than only those near the capital.

The date moved in 1968. The Uniform Monday Holiday Act — Public Law 90-363, enacted June 28, 1968 and effective January 1, 1971 — reorganized the federal calendar around three-day weekends. It shifted Washington's Birthday from February 22 to the third Monday in February, moved Memorial Day from May 30 to the last Monday in May, moved Veterans Day from November 11 to the fourth Monday in October, and added Columbus Day on the second Monday in October. Veterans Day was returned to November 11 by a 1975 law. Washington's Birthday was not moved back, and has not fallen on February 22 since.

The name never changed, and the National Archives is blunt about it: neither Congress nor any president has ever stipulated that the holiday be called President's Day. The name was floated in 1951 and spread through retail advertising in the 1980s. The statute, 5 U.S.C. 6103, still reads "Washington's Birthday," and the Office of Personnel Management says the same when asked directly. The gap between the legal name and the one on the mattress circular is the most interesting thing about this holiday.

Washington was born on February 22, 1732 by the Gregorian calendar. Britain and its colonies did not adopt that calendar until 1752; under the Julian calendar in use when he was born, the date was February 11.

### How to observe

Read Washington's Farewell Address, or at least the passages on faction and foreign entanglement. The Senate still has one of its own members read all 7,641 words aloud in the chamber each year around the holiday, alternating between the parties, and has done so every year since 1896 — the tradition traces to a single reading on February 22, 1862, revived in 1888. The reader then signs a leather-bound notebook kept by the Secretary of the Senate and adds a few remarks, which makes the book a one-senator-a-year commentary on American politics going back to 1900.

Go to Mount Vernon. Washington's estate in Virginia admits visitors free on the holiday and treats it as an actual birthday: a wreath-laying at his tomb, cannon firings by the Presidential Salute Battery, fife and drum, a Revolutionary War encampment on the field, and an open house at the research library. Mansion tours are timed and first come, first served, with waits of two to three hours — check the year's schedule before driving out.
timeline:
- February 22, 1732 — George Washington is born, by the Gregorian calendar; under the Julian calendar then in use in the British colonies the date was February 11.
- January 31, 1879 — Congress adds February 22 to the holidays observed by federal employees in the District of Columbia. The act does not require that they be paid for it.
- 1885 — Congress requires pay for federal holidays and extends them to all federal employees, not only those near Washington.
- 1951 — The name "Presidents' Day" is proposed. The federal government never adopts it.
- June 28, 1968 — The Uniform Monday Holiday Act (Pub. L. 90-363) moves Washington's Birthday to the third Monday in February, along with Memorial Day and Veterans Day, and adds Columbus Day. It takes effect January 1, 1971.
- September 18, 1975 — Pub. L. 94-97 returns Veterans Day to November 11. Washington's Birthday stays on its Monday.
faq:
Is the holiday officially called Presidents' Day?
No. The federal holiday is "Washington's Birthday" in 5 U.S.C. 6103, and the Office of Personnel Management gives that as the official name. The National Archives notes that neither Congress nor any president has ever stipulated the name "President's Day." It became the common name through holiday sales advertising in the 1980s, after being proposed and rejected in 1951.

Can the holiday fall on Washington's actual birthday?
No. The third Monday in February can only fall between February 15 and February 21. February 22 is outside that range, so since the Monday rule took effect in 1971 the holiday has never landed on the date it was created to mark.

Why is it on a Monday?
The Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968, effective January 1, 1971, moved several federal holidays to Mondays to create three-day weekends. Washington's Birthday was one of four holidays it changed.

Does the federal holiday honor all the presidents?
Not in law. 5 U.S.C. 6103 names Washington's Birthday and nobody else. The broader meaning came from popular and commercial use rather than from Congress, and states are free to name and observe their own February holidays differently.

Is it a federal holiday?
Yes — one of the eleven legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103. Federal offices, banks and post offices close on the third Monday in February.

- U.S. Senate, Washington's Farewell Address — https://www.senate.gov/about/traditions-symbols/washingtons-farewell-address.htm → the first Senate reading on February 22, 1862 by Secretary of the Senate John W. Forney; the 1888 revival; the unbroken annual reading since 1896; the 7,641-word length; the alternation between parties; and the leather-bound notebook kept by the Secretary of the Senate, first signed in 1900.
- Mount Vernon Ladies' Association, Washington's Birthday Celebration — https://www.mountvernon.org/plan-your-visit/calendar/events/washingtons-birthday-celebration/ → free admission on the holiday; the wreath-laying at Washington's tomb, Presidential Salute Battery cannon firings, Fife and Drum performance, Revolutionary War encampment, and library open house; timed first-come mansion tours with waits of two to three hours.

The 1885 act and the 1975 Veterans Day law are given by date only, because the sources above do not supply the 1885 public law number. Mount Vernon's free-admission and program details are documented for the 2026 observance; the schedule is set each year, so it is worth checking before a trip.

name: Small Business Saturday
description: Small Business Saturday falls on the Saturday after Thanksgiving, wedged between Black Friday and Cyber Monday, and it was created by a credit card company. American Express launched it in 2010, during the recession, to push some of the holiday weekend's spending toward small and local businesses. Unlike the two days flanking it, it has been formally designated by the United States Senate, repeatedly and by name.
body:
### History

The day is a corporate initiative that acquired an official endorsement. American Express says it created Small Business Saturday "in the midst of the recession in 2010," placing it on the Saturday after Thanksgiving "to encourage people to Shop Small and bring more holiday shopping to small businesses." The company describes the Saturday as one part of a larger, year-round Shop Small movement, and says the first one, in 2010, was a success.

The following year it entered the congressional record. On November 10, 2011, Senator Mary Landrieu and thirty-two co-sponsors from both parties submitted S.Res. 320, which was considered and agreed to. It designated November 26, 2011 as "Small Business Saturday" and supported efforts "to encourage consumers to shop locally" and "to increase awareness of the value of locally owned small businesses and the impact of locally owned small businesses on the economy of the United States." American Express's account that the Senate passed a resolution in 2011 matches the record.

It then became a habit. The Senate designated the day again for November 24, 2012, in S.Res. 589, sponsored by Senator Olympia Snowe, and for November 29, 2014, in S.Res. 548, sponsored by Senator Maria Cantwell. Each was considered and agreed to. The resolutions make their case in findings rather than rhetoric: the 2014 text counts 28,200,000 small businesses in the United States, employing more than 48 percent of private-sector workers, paying more than 42 percent of private-sector payroll, and responsible for 63 percent of the net new jobs created between 1993 and 2013.

Two things are worth noting about the pairing. None of those resolutions mentions American Express. And the company's own pages, which state the founding year plainly, do not give the calendar date of that first Small Business Saturday in 2010.

### How to observe

The instruction in the Senate's own language is the simplest one available: shop locally. The practical version is to spend where the owner is on the premises — a hardware store, a bookshop, a repair counter, a restaurant that is not a franchise — and to do it on an errand you were going to run anyway, rather than as a gesture.

Two things are worth more to a small business than one Saturday's purchase. The first is a review: a few specific sentences on whichever platform your neighbors actually read. The second is a gift card or a deposit against future work, which moves cash into the business now, in the season when it needs it.

If you run a small business yourself, the Senate resolutions are public documents you can quote in your own promotion, and they cost nothing to use. American Express's Shop Small program is a sponsor's marketing platform, which you may or may not want to join. The day works either way.
timeline:
- 2010 — American Express creates Small Business Saturday, placing it on the Saturday after Thanksgiving, and the first one is held that November.
- November 10, 2011 — Senator Mary Landrieu and thirty-two co-sponsors submit S.Res. 320; it is considered and agreed to, designating November 26, 2011 as Small Business Saturday.
- September 22, 2012 — S.Res. 589, sponsored by Senator Olympia Snowe, is considered and agreed to, designating November 24, 2012.
- September 16, 2014 — S.Res. 548, sponsored by Senator Maria Cantwell, is considered and agreed to, designating November 29, 2014, with findings counting 28,200,000 small businesses in the United States.
- Since 2010 — American Express describes the Saturday as one part of its broader, year-round Shop Small movement.
faq:
Is Small Business Saturday a federal holiday?
No. The 11 legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) do not include it. The Senate has designated particular dates as Small Business Saturday by resolution in several years, which is a formal expression of support rather than the creation of a holiday.

Who started Small Business Saturday?
American Express, in 2010. The company says it created the day "in the midst of the recession in 2010" and set it on the Saturday after Thanksgiving. It remains a sponsored initiative, though the Senate resolutions endorsing the date do not mention the company.

When is Small Business Saturday?
The Saturday after Thanksgiving. Because federal law places Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday in November, the Saturday falls between November 24 and November 30.

Has Congress officially recognized it?
The Senate has, several times, one year at a time. S.Res. 320 designated November 26, 2011; S.Res. 589 designated November 24, 2012; S.Res. 548 designated November 29, 2014. Each was considered and agreed to. These are Senate resolutions rather than statutes, and they oblige no one to do anything.

How much do people spend on Small Business Saturday?
This page does not give a figure. Spending and participation totals for the day circulate widely every year, but none could be traced to a primary record for this page, so none is published here rather than repeating a number that cannot be checked.

name: St. Patrick's Day
description: St. Patrick's Day falls on March 17, the traditional date of the death of Ireland's patron saint, and it is one of the few holidays Americans largely built for themselves. The parades, the green river in Chicago, the corned beef: almost all of it took shape in American cities, among Irish immigrants who were not especially welcome in them.
body:
### History

What is reliably known about Patrick comes mostly from Patrick. His Confessio, published with its manuscripts and translations by the Royal Irish Academy, is a first-person account and strikingly plain: he calls himself a sinner and a simple country person, the least of all believers, and says many look down on him. He names his father, Calpornius, a deacon, and his grandfather Potitus, a priest, and places his family home near somewhere he calls Bannavem Taburniae. He says he was about sixteen when he was taken prisoner there. The Library of Congress notes that legend holds he died on March 17, around 492 — the date the feast commemorates.

The stories most people can recite — the shamrock explaining the Trinity, the snakes driven into the sea — are later traditions. This page has no primary source for either, so it will not tell you when they began.

The American holiday is better documented, and it is an immigrant story before it is an Irish one. The Charitable Irish Society, founded in Boston in 1737 and still describing itself as the oldest Irish society in the Americas, has held a March 17 dinner since its founding; one of its two original purposes was relieving suffering among Irish arrivals in need. Parades came later: the Library of Congress dates New York's official parade to March 17, 1766, with an unofficial march in 1762, suggests Boston's may go back to 1775, and puts Savannah's at 1824.

Then came the famine. Irish immigration rose sharply in the 1840s after the potato famine of 1845–49, which killed more than a million people. Many arrivals met economic discrimination and open prejudice from an Anglo-Saxon Protestant majority hostile both to the Irish and to Catholicism, which is part of why a parade was never only a celebration. When New York's St. Patrick's Cathedral was completed in 1879, the route was extended up Fifth Avenue so the archbishop and clergy could review it from in front of the church.

### How to observe

Read Patrick in his own voice. The Royal Irish Academy's Confessio site carries the Latin alongside English translations and the manuscripts that preserve the text. It is short, and the distance between the man who wrote it and the figure on the parade float is the most interesting thing about the day.

Find out what your city's parade actually is; many are older than their green-beer reputation and are still run by Irish-American societies. In Chicago the river is dyed by the plumbers' union: NBC Chicago reports that plumbers in the 1960s used orange dye to trace a leak, saw it turn the water green, and the head of Local 130 then proposed doing it deliberately, with the agreement of his friend Mayor Richard J. Daley. The dyeing follows the parade weekend rather than March 17 — in 2026 it began at 10 a.m. on March 14.
timeline:
- 1737 — The Charitable Irish Society is founded in Boston and begins holding a St. Patrick's Day dinner on March 17.
- 1762 — An unofficial St. Patrick's Day march is held in New York City.
- 1766 — New York City's official St. Patrick's Day parade dates from March 17 of this year.
- 1845–49 — Ireland's potato famine kills more than a million people and drives a sharp rise in Irish immigration to the United States.
- 1879 — St. Patrick's Cathedral is completed in New York and the parade is extended up Fifth Avenue so the archbishop and clergy can review it.
- 1960s — Chicago plumbers find that orange leak-tracing dye turns the river green; the head of Plumbers' Local 130 proposes doing it on purpose for St. Patrick's Day.
faq:
Is St. Patrick's Day a federal holiday in the United States?
No. March 17 does not appear on the Office of Personnel Management's list of federal holidays, set by 5 U.S.C. 6103. Federal offices, banks, and the mail all run normally.

Is it a public holiday in Ireland?
Yes, one of the country's ten. If it falls on a day you would not normally work you still get public-holiday benefit, but there is no automatic legal right to take the next working day off.

Which American city had the first St. Patrick's Day parade?
It is genuinely contested, and the answer depends on what counts as a parade. The Library of Congress dates New York's official parade to March 17, 1766 and an unofficial march to 1762, and says Boston's may go back to 1775. The frequently cited Boston 1737 is the year the Charitable Irish Society was founded and began its March 17 dinner — a banquet, not a parade.

Did St. Patrick use a shamrock to explain the Trinity?
Not in anything he wrote. The Confessio, his own surviving account of his life, does not contain the story. It is a later tradition, and this page has no primary source for when it started.

Why is the Chicago River green?
Because the plumbers' union dyes it. NBC Chicago reports that plumbers in the 1960s used orange dye to find a leak, noticed it turned the water green, and the head of Local 130 proposed doing it on purpose, with Mayor Richard J. Daley's agreement.

- Library of Congress, Today in History — March 17 — https://www.loc.gov/item/today-in-history/march-17/ → St. Patrick as patron saint of Ireland and the legend that he died on March 17, circa 492; New York City's official parade dating to March 17, 1766 and an unofficial march in 1762; Boston's parade possibly dating to March 17, 1775; Savannah's to March 17, 1824; the 1879 completion of St. Patrick's Cathedral and the parade's extension up Fifth Avenue so the archbishop and clergy could review it; the sharp rise in Irish immigration in the 1840s after the 1845–49 potato famine, which killed more than a million people; and the economic discrimination and prejudice Irish arrivals met from an Anglo-Saxon Protestant majority hostile to the Irish and to Catholicism.
- Royal Irish Academy, Saint Patrick's Confessio (St Patrick's Confessio HyperStack) — https://www.confessio.ie/ → the Confessio as Patrick's own first-person account, published by the Royal Irish Academy with the Latin text, English and other translations, and the medieval manuscripts that preserve it; Patrick calling himself a sinner, a simple country person and the least of all believers, and saying many look down on him; his father Calpornius a deacon and grandfather Potitus a priest; the family home near Bannavem Taburniae; his capture there at about sixteen.
- Charitable Irish Society, About Us — https://charitableirishsociety.org/About-Us → founding in Boston in 1737; the two original purposes, including relieving suffering and aiding members and other worthy recipients in need; the St. Patrick's Day dinner held on March 17 since its founding; and the society's description of itself as the oldest Irish society in the Americas. Cited as the organization's own account of its history.
- Citizens Information (Ireland), Public holidays — https://www.citizensinformation.ie/en/employment/employment-rights-and-conditions/leave-and-holidays/public-holidays/ → St Patrick's Day, 17 March, as one of Ireland's ten public holidays; entitlement to public-holiday benefit when the day is not a normal working day, with no automatic legal entitlement to the next working day off.
- U.S. Office of Personnel Management, Federal Holidays — https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/federal-holidays/ → the eleven federal holidays established by 5 U.S.C. 6103, and the absence of March 17 from that list.
- NBC Chicago, Why does Chicago dye its river green for St. Patrick's Day? How the tradition began — https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/why-does-chicago-dye-its-river-green-for-st-patricks-day-how-the-tradition-began/3907795/ → plumbers in the 1960s using orange dye to find a broken pipe and seeing the water turn green; the head of Plumbers' Union Local 130 proposing the river be dyed before St. Patrick's Day; his call to his friend Mayor Richard J. Daley; and the 2026 dyeing beginning at 10 a.m. on March 14.

On the "first parade" question: the Library of Congress is followed throughout, and the frequently repeated Boston 1737 date is treated as the Charitable Irish Society's founding and dinner rather than a parade, per that society's own page. No aggregator claim is repeated. The shamrock and snake legends are left undated because no primary source for them was found.
